rv.q: As he did in Stratford last summer, McAnuff embraces one of the musical theater’s most unusual, famous, bizarre, historically audacious and, in this instance, thoroughly enjoyable properties with a production remarkably in sync with the material.
Honestly, it's enough to give rock opera a good name.
The new Broadway revival of 'Jesus Christ Superstar' is a sleek, well-sung production that succeeds in making Andrew Lloyd Webber's 1970 rock opera feel fresh again.

If this rock-opera reimagining of the “Greatest Story Ever Told” is far from ageless and seems unlikely to spark major new insights for believers or non-believers, as a time-travel experience it offers plenty to enjoy.
If you like some fun in your "Superstar," however, the show that capped his final year as head of the Stratford Shakespeare Festival may feel pretty grandiose for much of the material.
In fact, all the bells and whistles on stage grow increasingly cloying and wearying.

The agonies of Jesus are terrible to behold, of course, but on a far more trivial level one of the agonies of “Jesus Christ Superstar” is the unhappy combination of Mr. Lloyd Webber’s stick-in-your-head melodies and the often flat-footed lyrics they are wedded to.

This Jesus doesn't live, he merely deafens us, and although Forster makes plenty of noise, he has only two facial expressions (pained, or faintly smouldering like a bit of damp kindling) and he lacks the charisma to persuade that he could be the leader of a revolutionary movement.
McAnuff deserves credit for an admirable job of pacing—the show flies by at a little less than two hours—and a talented cast displays an array of powerful rock voices.
McAnuff's presented the show in a sleek, clean way that reduces gimmicks and makes it all move very quickly, while getting to the heart of the betrayed-icon rock operatics.
Though intermittently moving and seldom dull, this account of Jesus' final days on Earth isn't recommended to anyone with a low tolerance for pomp.
In short, the production is for teenagers and their allies.
The final sequence had me holding my breath so long I nearly turned as purple as the suit Paul Tazewell has designed for Pilate.

cn.t: McAnuff's revival divides critics with its hyper-kinetic spectacle and modern tech, though most praise the strong vocal performances. Some find it sleek and energetic, while others feel it over-relies on flashy gimmicks.

sg.ra: For MJ the Musical's dance-heavy choreography, Center Orchestra rows A-H sit entirely in front of the mezzanine overhang (which begins at row J) and deliver head-on sightlines of the performers' feet — critical for a Michael Jackson dance biomusical. Row A seats 107-110 are frequently cited as the theatre's best, but rows C-D balance proximity with neck-angle comfort.

Because Neil Simon's orchestra is unusually deep (25 rows, A-Z) and the mezzanine overhang only starts cutting the top of the stage noticeably by row S, rows H-P give you full head-on views with no overhang effect at non-premium pricing — a specific quirk of this house's long orchestra footprint.

The mezzanine overhang is felt from row J onward and by rows S-Z it actively cuts off the top of the stage per SeatPlan's orchestra guide — a real issue for MJ the Musical, which uses tall set pieces and lifts. Unique to Neil Simon because the orchestra runs all the way to row Z, pushing rear seats deep under the overhang.

Front Center Mezzanine rows A-B give an elevated, unobstructed sweep — particularly valuable at Neil Simon because MJ the Musical uses formation choreography that reads better from above. Tripadvisor users confirm no obstruction issues at front mezz (photo cited from row A seat 103). Row A also has the best legroom in the mezzanine.

Specific Neil Simon quirk: Left and Right Mezzanine rows H and L sit directly behind railings that border the internal staircase, making legroom 'very tight' — SeatPlan calls out seats H1-7 and L9-15 by number. This is a house-specific hazard, not the generic 'Broadway legroom is tight' complaint.

Rear mezzanine at Neil Simon has a shallow rake — a specific architectural quirk noted by SeatPlan — so rows S-U feel distant and lose detail on the stage front, and the mezzanine's own underside can minor-obstruct the back-row view. For MJ's facial-expression moments in 'Man in the Mirror' numbers this is a real detriment.

Three boxes are staggered off the Left Mezzanine at Neil Simon — a specific architectural feature of this house — and SeatPlan explicitly states the viewing experience 'isn't the best' because the angle is fully side-on. Priced as premium but not worth it for a dance musical where frontal sightlines matter.
